round_and_level: PM round or hiring-manager round; PM to SPM (needs ops and supply-chain fluency)
difficulty: Hard - the drop is confined to one segment (new dark-store polygons), so generic funnel answers fail. The root cause sits where catalogue, store assignment and fees meet, and needs ops knowledge
market_and_industry: India; quick commerce (10-30 min grocery and essentials). New polygons are mostly metro outskirts and Tier-2 cities (e.g. Indore, Lucknow, Thane edge), on mid-range Android phones, with Hindi and vernacular users and lower AOV
exact_prompt: You're the PM for checkout at Blinkit. Cart abandonment is spiking, but only in dark-store polygons we've launched in the last 6-8 weeks. Mature polygons look normal. Find the cause.
source_and_verification: Synthetic (written by the authors in Blinkit/Zepto style; not reported from a real interview). Built on the local Blinkit teardown (blinkit_product_teardown/teardown_acquisition_coverage.md, data as of Q1 FY27, Oct 2026). Similar real RCA prompts include Zepto/Blinkit 'orders dropped in one city' questions on NextLeap (https://nextleap.app/interview-preparation/product-management/questions/topic/rca). Year: 2026.
context_as_of: From the Blinkit teardown (Q1 FY27, Apr-Jun 2026, Eternal disclosures, compiled Oct 2026): 2,443 dark stores in Jun 2026, +200 net in Q1 FY27, target about 3,000 by Mar 2027. NOV Rs 17,132 crore (+86% YoY). Adjusted EBITDA Rs 102 crore, about 0.6% of NOV. AOV Rs 518 (down from Rs 525). About 1,550 orders and about Rs 8 lakh NOV per store per day. Capex per store Rs 2.5 crore (up from Rs 1 crore). Assortment about 80k SKUs in Delhi-NCR vs about 20k in smaller cities. Outside the top 8 cities Blinkit covers under 30% of pincodes. Blinkit dropped its '10-minute' claim in Jan 2026. Industry: about 9 in 10 new stores in Apr-Jun 2026 opened in already-served pincodes (Bernstein, indicative), so new polygons often carve out of an existing store's area. Stale-risk flags: Q2 FY27 numbers (Oct 2026) were not in the teardown; Blinkit is reported under Eternal (formerly Zomato).
regulatory_context: CCPA Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023 (drip pricing, basket sneaking, false urgency) apply directly: a fee or item change that appears only at checkout is both an abandonment driver and a compliance risk. Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) rules on MRP display, and FSSAI/state FDA licensing for each new dark store, can delay perishable categories in new stores. FDI rules (inventory-led model under an Indian-owned-and-controlled structure) and state gig-worker welfare levies on per-order cost are background, not causes.
public_data_anchors: From blinkit_product_teardown/teardown_acquisition_coverage.md (Eternal Q1 FY27 letter and analyst reports, as of Jun-Oct 2026): 2,443 stores; +200 net stores per quarter; NOV Rs 17,132 crore; AOV Rs 518; about 1,550 orders per store per day; Rs 2.5 crore capex per store; about 80k vs about 20k SKUs metro vs smaller city; under 30% pincode coverage outside the top 8 cities; household QC penetration about 34% in Delhi-NCR vs about 6% in an average Tier-2 city; Blinkit in-stock about 94.4% vs Flipkart Minutes 88.7%; top-5 metros about 4,300 stores against about 3,600 of profitable capacity (Bernstein, Jul 2026). All funnel and abandonment numbers in the exhibits are illustrative.
framework_applied: RCA framework (frameworks.md section 4). Step 1 Clarify - metric: cart abandonment = sessions with at least one item in the cart and no order placed within 30 min, divided by sessions with a cart; time frame: rose over 6-8 weeks as each new store launched, a step change at each launch; scope: only polygons live under 8 weeks (about 60 stores), both new cities and metro carve-outs; mature polygons flat. Step 2a Data: check that new stores have the same event schema, and that session stitching isn't broken by the polygon reassignment; abandonment is confirmed by low orders per active user. Step 2b Internal: funnel (browse, add to cart, view cart, checkout, pay) shows drop-off at 'view cart'; product cause is the catalogue being served from the parent store while the cart re-validates against the new store's thin inventory, plus a long-distance fee for edge addresses. Step 2c External: competitor entry (Flipkart Minutes, Amazon Now in Tier-2), local festival or monsoon, payment outages; checked against matched controls. Step 2d Behaviour: new users in new cities have lower AOV and hit small-cart fees; they are also trial users comparing prices. Step 3 Hypothesise-test with wide splits (new city vs carve-out, new vs existing user, step of the funnel). Step 4 Land: inventory mismatch between browse and cart during the polygon handover, compounded by fees at checkout; validate by cart-edit events and A/B on catalogue binding; fix by binding browse to the serving store and making fees visible earlier.

clarifying_questions.q: How do we define cart abandonment - cart created but no order within the session, or within some time window?
clarifying_questions.a: A session with at least one item in the cart and no order within 30 minutes, divided by all sessions with a cart.

clarifying_questions.q: How big is the spike, and how many polygons count as 'new'?
clarifying_questions.a: Mature polygons sit at about 38%. The roughly 60 polygons launched in the last 8 weeks are at about 61%.

clarifying_questions.q: Are the new polygons new cities, or carve-outs from existing stores in cities we already serve?
clarifying_questions.a: A mix: about 40% are new Tier-2 cities, about 60% split an existing metro store's area.

clarifying_questions.q: Is it all new polygons, or does it fade as a store ages?
clarifying_questions.a: It's high in week 1-4 and eases a bit by week 8, but stays well above mature stores.

clarifying_questions.q: Does it affect new users only, or also existing Blinkit users whose address moved into a new polygon?
clarifying_questions.a: Both. Existing users in carve-outs are surprisingly hit hard.

clarifying_questions.q: Where in the funnel do users drop - before checkout, at the payment step, or after payment fails?
clarifying_questions.a: Good question. You can ask for the funnel.

clarifying_questions.q: Any recent pricing, fee or app changes, or competitor launches in those areas?
clarifying_questions.a: No app release targeted these stores. Fees follow the standard rules. Competitors are present in some of them.

clarifying_questions.q: What's the business goal - conversion in new stores, or new-store payback?
clarifying_questions.a: Payback. New stores need to reach throughput fast; abandonment is slowing the ramp.

interviewer_data_reveals.exhibit: Exhibit 4 - Root mechanism found in logs (illustrative)
interviewer_data_reveals.data: For carve-out addresses, the home and search feed is still served from the parent store's catalogue (about 9,000 live SKUs) because the catalogue cache is keyed on the old store-to-pincode map. The cart re-checks stock against the new store (about 3,500 live SKUs in week 2, ramping). Items that were shown as in stock disappear at the cart. In new Tier-2 cities, the cause is thin assortment plus a small-cart fee: AOV is about Rs 340 against a Rs 199 free-delivery threshold, with most carts sitting near the fee line.

Payment success rate same as mature (about 96%). No new app version in the window. Competitor launches (Flipkart Minutes, Amazon Now) overlap only about a third of the new polygons, and abandonment is just as high in non-overlap polygons. No festival or monsoon pattern; the spike follows store launch dates, not calendar dates.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Cart abandonment is spiking, but only in dark-store polygons we launched in the last 6-8 weeks. Find the cause.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: The fact that it's isolated to new polygons is a huge clue, so I'll keep that as my control. First the metric: is abandonment 'cart created, no order within the session'?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Cart with at least one item and no order within 30 minutes. Mature polygons are at about 38%, the roughly 60 new ones at about 61%.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Does it rise as each store launches, or did it start on one calendar date across all of them?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: It follows each launch date. High in the first weeks, easing slightly by week 8.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Then the cause is tied to the store's lifecycle, not a release or a calendar event. That makes a global app bug, a festival or a payment outage less likely. And are these new polygons new cities, or carve-outs from existing stores?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: About 60% are carve-outs in existing metros, 40% new Tier-2 cities.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text:
Here's my board:

Abandonment up in new polygons only
|- 1. Data: new stores mis-instrumented, sessions broken when an address is remapped
|- 2. Internal: catalogue vs inventory mismatch, thin assortment, ETA promise, fee stack (small-cart, long-distance), substitutions, payment
|- 3. External: competitor launches, local events, payment or maps outages
|- 4. Behaviour: new trial users comparing prices, lower AOV

Data first: do new stores use the same event schema, and are orders per user also low there?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Same schema, and yes, orders per active user are lower. It's real.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Good. Wide question next: where in the funnel is the extra drop?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Exhibit 1.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Opening the cart is normal, and payment start-to-order is close to normal. The gap is between 'opened cart' and 'reached checkout', 16 points worse. So something surprises the user when they look at the cart. Payment is out. What do users see when they open the cart?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Exhibit 2.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Three things stand out. 29% of carts get an 'items unavailable' banner versus 6% in mature stores, with almost 2 items removed. 22% see a longer ETA in the cart than on the home screen. And 34% get a long-distance or small-cart fee. Each is a broken promise at the cart. The unavailable items are the strangest, because we shouldn't be showing items we don't have. Does it differ between carve-outs and new cities?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Exhibit 3. Carve-outs are worse: 64% abandonment, 36% of carts with items made unavailable. New cities: 56% and 18%.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: That's the reverse of what I'd expect if assortment were the only issue. New Tier-2 cities have the thinnest assortment, yet carve-outs in metros are worse. My hypothesis: in carve-outs, the browse feed is still served from the old parent store, while the cart is checked against the new store. Users browse the parent's full shelf, add items, then the cart drops what the new store doesn't stock yet. Is the catalogue binding at the store or the pincode level?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Exhibit 4. You're right. The catalogue cache is keyed on the old store-to-pincode map. Browse shows about 9,000 SKUs from the parent store; the new store has about 3,500 live in week 2.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: That explains why it eases by week 8: the new store's assortment ramps up and the gap shrinks. And the ETA jump fits too, because home shows the parent store's ETA and the cart recalculates from the new store, whose riders are still ramping. In new Tier-2 cities, with no parent store, what's driving it?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Thin assortment and fees. AOV is about Rs 340, and a lot of carts sit just under the free-delivery threshold.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: So in Tier-2 it's the fee stack hitting trial users with small baskets, and it's revealed late, which is also a CCPA drip-pricing risk. Quick external sweep: competitors, local events?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Exhibit 5. Abandonment is just as high where there's no competitor overlap. No calendar pattern. Payment success is normal.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: Then external factors are ruled out. Here's my landing. Root cause #1, carve-outs (about 60% of new polygons and the worst abandonment): a catalogue-to-store binding bug during polygon handover. Users browse the parent store's shelf, and the cart re-validates against the new store's thin, ramping inventory, so items vanish and the ETA jumps at the cart. #2, new Tier-2 cities: a thin shelf plus a small-cart or long-distance fee shown only at the cart, against a low AOV of about Rs 340. #3, contributing everywhere: new riders in the polygon mean longer real ETAs in the first weeks. To validate: (1) abandonment for carts with at least one system-removed item versus none, within the same new store; (2) a holdout where browse is bound to the serving store, which should close most of the carve-out gap; (3) Tier-2 abandonment by distance from the fee threshold. Fixes: bind browse and search to the actual serving store from day 1, and invalidate the cache on the polygon remap; for the transition, show 'available from tomorrow' instead of silently removing items, or fulfil from the parent store with a longer ETA; show fees and the free-delivery bar on the home screen, not first in the cart; and in Tier-2, a launch-period lower threshold, funded as CAC. Prevention: a store-launch checklist with a catalogue-parity check and a launch dashboard for cart-edit rate per new store.

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Interviewer
solution_walkthrough.text: Why not just stock the new store fully before launch?

solution_walkthrough.speaker: Candidate
solution_walkthrough.text: That's the ideal, but it ties up working capital in a Rs 2.5 crore store before we know demand, and it isn't the bug. Even a fully stocked new store will have some differences from the parent. The product fix is making browse honest about what the serving store has. Ops can then use cart-add data on items the new store doesn't stock as a demand signal to decide what to stock next.

answer_and_recommendation: Ranked causes (illustrative magnitudes): (1) Catalogue-to-store binding mismatch during polygon handover in metro carve-outs. Browse is served from the parent store's cached catalogue (about 9,000 SKUs) while the cart re-validates against the new store (about 3,500 SKUs in week 2), so 36% of carts lose items and the ETA jumps at the cart; this is about 60% of the excess abandonment. (2) In new Tier-2 cities, a thin assortment plus a small-cart or long-distance fee revealed only at the cart, against a low AOV of about Rs 340. (3) Real early-week ETA inflation from a ramping rider fleet. Recommendation: bind browse and search to the serving store on day 1, with cache invalidation on polygon remaps; replace silent removals with 'arrives tomorrow' or a parent-store fallback with honest ETA; surface fees and the free-delivery threshold on the home screen (also CCPA dark-pattern hygiene); run a launch-period threshold offer in Tier-2, budgeted as CAC; add catalogue parity to the store-launch checklist. Risks: binding browse to a thin store lowers add-to-cart and makes the store look empty (mitigate with 'coming soon' shelves and notify-me); parent-store fallback raises delivery cost (cap it by distance and time window); lower thresholds hit unit economics at a 0.6% EBITDA margin (time-box and limit to first orders). Closing line: 'Users aren't abandoning because they don't want Blinkit in new areas. They're abandoning because we show them a shelf the new store doesn't have, then take it away at the cart.'
counter_metrics_guardrails: Guardrails: add-to-cart rate and sessions per user in new polygons (an honest, thinner catalogue must not kill browsing); in-stock rate and fill rate at the serving store; delivery cost per order and ETA adherence for parent-store fallback orders; AOV and contribution margin per order (threshold offers must not destroy economics); new-store throughput ramp (orders/day at week 4 and 8) and payback; complaint rate on fees and substitutions; CCPA dark-pattern audit pass. Counter-metric: abandonment in mature polygons, to confirm the catalogue change doesn't regress them.

follow_up_twists.twist: The binding fix shipped, carve-out abandonment fell, but add-to-cart also fell 12%.
follow_up_twists.response: That's expected from an honest shelf. I'd watch orders per session (the true outcome), add 'coming soon' plus notify-me on missing SKUs, and use the notify-me data to prioritise what the new store stocks first.

follow_up_twists.twist: Abandonment is high in one specific new store only, not all new ones.
follow_up_twists.response: Then it's store-local: check the polygon geometry (a river or highway inside the polygon inflating ETAs), the rider supply at that store, its in-stock rate and any FSSAI licence delays on perishables.

follow_up_twists.twist: Leadership asks if we should pause new store launches.
follow_up_twists.response: No. The cause is a launch-process bug, not demand. Fix the handover and fee visibility, and gate future launches on a catalogue-parity check rather than pausing growth.

common_pitfalls: 1) Blaming competitors (Flipkart Minutes, Amazon Now in Tier-2) without a control. Abandonment is just as high where they aren't present. 2) Going straight to 'thin assortment' as the answer. It doesn't explain why metro carve-outs are worse than brand-new cities. 3) Treating it as a payment or checkout UX problem. The payment step is normal; the break is at cart open. 4) Recommending discounts first. That treats the symptom and burns margin at about 0.6% EBITDA of NOV without fixing the broken promise between browse and cart.
